result:
I now have a complete picture of both the write path and the query path. Let me write the explanation.

## How editing an issue title reaches search moments later

**The write path — keeping the index in step**

Nothing writes directly to the search index at edit time. When a colleague edits a title, the Server Action in `src/actions/issues/update-issue.ts` (`updateIssueAction` → the wrapped `run`) checks `can(actor, "issue:update", ...)` and then calls `updateIssue()` in `src/server/services/issue-service.ts:83`. That function does the tenant check (`assertOrgScope`), permission check (`assertCan`), and archived-state check (`assertNotArchived`), persists the change via `issueRepo.updateIssue(input)`, and — critically — calls `emit("issue.updated", { issueId, projectId, changedFields, ... })` from `src/lib/event-bus.ts`. It never touches search itself; the row update and the event are the only two things it does.

`emit()` (`src/lib/event-bus.ts:54`) looks up every handler subscribed to `"issue.updated"` and runs them via `Promise.allSettled`, so a slow or throwing search listener can never fail the caller's update or block sibling listeners (activity log, webhooks, usage tracking).

The search side subscribes at process start: `src/server/services/event-registry.ts`'s `registerEventHandlers()` (invoked once from `src/instrumentation.ts`) calls `registerSearchListeners()` in `src/server/services/search-service.ts:137`. That function does `subscribe("issue.updated", async (payload) => { const issue = await issueRepo.findIssueById(...); if (issue) await indexIssue(...); })`. Note it deliberately **re-reads the issue row** from `issue-repository` rather than trusting the event payload's `changedFields` — the comment at `search-service.ts:132` explains this is so a partially-applied write is never indexed as if it fully succeeded.

`indexIssue()` (`search-service.ts:88`) then calls `searchRepo.upsertSearchDocument(orgId, "issue", issue.id, [issue.title, issue.description ?? ""].join("\n"), issue.projectId)`. That lands in `src/server/repositories/search-repository.ts:18`, which looks for an existing row keyed by `(orgId, subjectKind, subjectId)` — not by search-index row id — and either `UPDATE`s its `content`/`projectId`/`indexedAt` or inserts a new row. The upsert is keyed this way specifically because the indexer is invoked on every write and must be idempotent (comment at line 14-17).

**What's stored:** the `searchIndex` table (`src/server/db/schema`, `SearchIndexRow`) holds one denormalized row per subject: `id`, `orgId`, `subjectKind` (`issue`/`comment`/`project`), `subjectId`, `projectId` (nullable), `content` — literally `title + "\n" + description` concatenated as plain text — and `indexedAt`. There's no separate tokenized/inverted index; `content` is just raw text matched later with SQL `LIKE`.

So end to end: **edit → `updateIssueAction` → `updateIssue()` (issue-service.ts) writes the row and `emit("issue.updated")` → event bus fans out → search-service's subscriber re-fetches the issue and calls `indexIssue()` → `upsertSearchDocument()` updates the `searchIndex` row.** All of this happens synchronously within the same `await emit(...)` in `updateIssue()`, so by the time `updateIssueAction` returns to the client, the index row is already updated (there's no queue/async worker in between for this path — that's reserved for `search.reindex_requested`, used for backfills/drift repair, handled by the same `indexIssue()` call at `search-service.ts:170`).

**The query path — and when it's refused**

The colleague's search reaches `search()` in `search-service.ts:46` via one of two duplicated entry points that both must agree on gating (comment in `src/app/api/search/route.ts` says this is deliberate — "neither entry point can be the lenient one"):
- `searchAction` in `src/actions/search/search.ts` (Server Action, used by the search page/command palette on submit)
- `GET` in `src/app/api/search/route.ts` (plain fetch route, used by the palette on every keystroke)

Both first check `can(actor, "org:read", ...)`, look up the org via `getOrganizationSummary`, build a feature-flag context with `buildFlagContext`, and narrow `kinds` to `["issue"]` unless `advanced_search` is enabled — then call `search(actor, input)`.

Inside `search()` (`search-service.ts:46-86`), a valid-looking query can still be refused at several distinct points, in order:

1. **Tenant mismatch** — `assertOrgScope(actor, input.orgId)` throws a `TenantScopeError` if the actor's own `orgId` doesn't match the org being queried (`src/lib/tenant.ts:28`).
2. **Permission check** — `assertCan(actor, "issue:read", orgResource(input.orgId))` throws `PermissionDeniedError` if the actor lacks `issue:read` on that org (`src/lib/permissions.ts:150`, via `explain()`).
3. **Rate limit** — `consumeRateLimit(input.orgId, "search:query")` (`src/lib/rate-limit.ts`) is a token-bucket keyed by `(orgId, "search:query")`, base capacity 120 tokens refilling 60/minute, scaled by the org's plan (`configFor`, via `getPlanLimits(plan).apiRequestsPerHour`). If the bucket is empty, `search()` throws `"Search rate limit reached; try again after ${resetAt}"` — this is the case where a perfectly well-formed, authorized query is refused purely because too many were fired too quickly (e.g. the palette firing on every keystroke).
4. **Field-scoped syntax gated by plan** — if `input.q` contains a `:` (e.g. `status:done`) and the `advanced_search` feature flag (`isEnabled`, `src/lib/feature-flags.ts:21`, plan/role/percentage-based strategies) isn't enabled for that org/actor, `search()` throws `"Field-scoped search is not included in this plan"` rather than silently treating the colon as literal text.

Only after passing all four gates does it call `searchRepo.searchDocuments(input)`, which builds a `LIKE '%q%'` predicate over `content`, filtered by `orgId` (`orgPredicate`), optionally by `kinds` and `projectId`, keyset-paginated and ordered by `indexedAt desc, id desc`. Results are mapped back in `search()` into `SearchHit`s — title is `content.split("\n")[0]`, which is exactly why the freshly-edited title shows up: it's literally the first line of the same `content` string `indexIssue()` just wrote.
